Medieval Philosophy. The Western philosophical tradition spanning roughly the fifth to fifteenth centuries, dominated by the integration of Aristotelian logic and Platonist metaphysics with Christian theology. The central problem was reconciling faith—revealed truth from scripture—with reason, philosophical argument and debate. Can God's existence be proved by reason alone, or is faith a separate faculty? Augustine, Aquinas, and Duns Scotus spent centuries answering this question, developing sophisticated logical systems and theological arguments. Medieval philosophy is often dismissed as dogmatic, but it was intellectually rigorous, created the university system, and invented scholastic disputation, the ancestor of academic discourse.

Scholasticism is the defining method. It uses Aristotle's logic of syllogism and Aquinas's synthesis of reason and revelation. A scholastic asks a question, marshals arguments for and against from authorities—scripture, Aristotle, church fathers—and resolves the tension using careful logical reasoning. This method dominated universities until the seventeenth century.

Augustine, living from three fifty-four to four thirty, attempted to reconcile Platonism with Christianity. God is the ultimate Form; the soul is immortal; the physical world is subordinate to the spiritual. His Confessions established autobiographical introspection as a philosophical genre. Thomas Aquinas, from twelve twenty-five to twelve seventy-four, synthesized Aristotle with theology. He argued that Aristotle's logic and metaphysics were not heretical but compatible with Christianity. He proved God's existence using Aristotle's five ways—arguments from motion, causation, contingency, perfection, and design.

The problem of universals dominated medieval logic. Whether abstract properties—redness, humanity—exist independently or are mental constructs remains contested. Realists said universals exist; nominalists said they are merely names; moderates like Aquinas sought middle ground.

Divine omniscience versus human free will was another great struggle. If God knows the future with certainty, can humans have genuine free choice? Medieval philosophers struggled to reconcile God's foreknowledge with human moral responsibility. Aquinas argued God exists outside time, so God's knowledge is not causal. Medieval philosophers rediscovered Aristotle through Arabic translations and commentaries by Averroes and Avicenna. This recovery of Aristotle in the twelfth to thirteenth centuries revolutionized medieval thought.

The university system emerged in the twelfth century at Bologna, Oxford, and Paris as an institutional home for scholastic philosophy and theology. Duns Scotus, from twelve sixty-six to thirteen oh-eight, challenged Aquinas. He argued reason cannot prove God's existence or many theological truths; faith and revelation are necessary. Scotism competed with Thomism for influence through the Renaissance.

Medieval philosophy connects to scholasticism, its defining method. Thomas Aquinas was the most influential medieval philosopher. Humanism emerged as a reaction against scholasticism's abstract logic. Aristotle's logic and metaphysics were recovered and integrated. Dante Alighieri drew on medieval frameworks for his epic poetry. Christianity shaped the theological context for all medieval philosophy. And medieval thinkers were reviving ancient Greek philosophy.
